notes.front: What is pricing?
notes.back: The process by which a business sets and displays the price at which it will sell its products and services.
notes.explanation: In setting prices a business weighs, among other things, its costs, the marketplace, competition, brand and product quality.
notes.example: Like choosing what goes on a menu, but deciding the number printed beside each dish.
notes.evidence: Pricing is the process whereby a business sets and displays the price at which it will sell its products and services and may be part of the business's marketing plan .

notes.front: How is a price set under cost-plus pricing?
notes.back: Direct material, direct labour and overhead costs are added together, then a markup percentage is applied to give a profit margin.
notes.explanation: It is a cost-based method: the starting point is what the product costs to make, not what customers think it is worth.
notes.example: Like a joiner who totals timber, hours and workshop rent for a table, then adds a fixed percentage on top.
notes.evidence: Cost-plus pricing is a cost-based method for setting the prices of goods and services. Under this approach, the direct material cost, direct labor cost, and overhead costs for a product are added together, and a markup percentage is applied (to create a profit margin) in order to derive the price of the product.

notes.front: What is value-based pricing?
notes.back: Pricing a product on the value it has for the customer, not on its production costs or any other factor.
notes.explanation: The perceived value depends on the alternatives open to the customer, so the seller must know how customers see those alternatives.
notes.example: Like cost-plus pricing turned round: a tax-return app is priced by the hours and fees it saves users, not by what it cost to code.
notes.evidence: Pricing a product based on the value the product has for the customer and not on its costs of production or any other factor.

notes.front: What is price skimming?
notes.back: Launching at a high price for the keenest buyers, then lowering it step by step as each layer of demand is used up.
notes.explanation: The name comes from skimming successive layers of cream, or customer segments, off the top of the market as prices fall.
notes.example: Like a concert promoter who sells the front rows first at a premium, then releases cheaper seats as the eager fans are served.
notes.evidence: Price skimming is a price strategy where a marketer initially offers an item at a high price so that consumers with the strongest desire and funds to purchase it will, and then as that demand is depleted the price gets lowered to the next layer of customer desire in the market.

notes.front: What is penetration pricing?
notes.back: Setting a new product's price low at first to reach a wide share of the market quickly and start word of mouth.
notes.explanation: It relies on customers switching to the new brand because of the lower price, and is most often tied to enlarging market share and gaining economies of scale.
notes.example: Like price skimming in reverse: a new meal-kit service starts cheap to win as many households as it can.
notes.evidence: Penetration pricing is a pricing strategy especially appropriate for new product pricing, where the price of a product is initially set low to rapidly reach a wide fraction of the market and initiate word of mouth promotion .

notes.front: What is psychological pricing, also called price ending or charm pricing?
notes.back: Pricing based on the theory that certain prices have a psychological impact, often using just-below prices such as £2.98.
notes.explanation: Under this method, the article says, retail prices are often set as just-below numbers, such as £2.98 rather than £3, which consumers tend to see as lower than they are.
notes.example: Like rounding a price, but in the other direction: a bookshop tags a paperback £7.99 rather than £8.
notes.evidence: Psychological pricing (also price ending or charm pricing ) is a pricing and marketing strategy based on the theory that certain prices have a psychological impact. In this pricing method, retail prices are often expressed as just-below numbers

notes.front: What is product bundling?
notes.back: Offering several products or services for sale as one combined package.
notes.explanation: A bundle may be called a package deal, a box set or, in publishing, an anthology; the article says it is common in many imperfectly competitive markets.
notes.example: Like buying a camera body and a lens separately, except the shop sells them together in one box at one price.
notes.evidence: In marketing , product bundling is offering several products or services for sale as one combined product or service package.

notes.front: What is a loss leader?
notes.back: A product sold below its minimum profit margin to stimulate sales of other, more profitable goods or services.
notes.explanation: It is called a leader because it is meant to lead to the sale of other goods, such as when it draws customers into a store.
notes.example: Like a free sample, but paid for: a hardware shop sells paint at a slim price so shoppers also pick up brushes and rollers.
notes.evidence: A loss leader (also leader [ 1 ] ) is a product sold at a price below its minimum profit margin to stimulate other sales of more profitable goods or services.

notes.front: What is product line pricing?
notes.back: Pricing products in the same category at different price levels to create different quality levels in customers' minds.
notes.explanation: It is used when a company has more than one product in a product line.
notes.example: Like shelves of one shampoo brand where the salon-style bottle, the everyday bottle and the value bottle each sit at their own price.
notes.evidence: Product line pricing is a product pricing strategy, used when a company has more than one product in a product line. [ 10 ] It is a process that traders adopt to separate products in the same category into various price groups, to create different quality levels in the customers’ minds.

notes.front: What is price lining?
notes.back: Pricing different products at a limited number of prices.
notes.explanation: The article says it makes prices easy to administer and lets companies predict their customers and profits more easily.
notes.example: Like a car park with only three tariffs, a stationer sells every notebook at one of three price points, whatever the design.
notes.evidence: Price lining is a method of pricing different products for a limited number of prices. This strategy allows ease of administering and companies are able to predict their markets of customers and profits much easier.

notes.front: What is captive pricing?
notes.back: Selling a basic product very cheaply, knowing buyers must purchase additional items to get its full value.
notes.explanation: Profit lost on the first item is won back on the add-ons, and the article says it works best when no similar competing products sit in the same price range.
notes.example: Like a loss leader, except the later purchases are locked in: a cheap coffee machine that only takes the maker's own pods.
notes.evidence: Captive pricing is a strategy drawing consumers’ interests and encouraging purchases by offering a basic product for a really low price, however, they will have to purchase additional items in order to obtain the full value of the product they have received.

notes.front: What is price elasticity of demand (PED)?
notes.back: A measure of how sensitive the quantity demanded is to price: the percentage change in quantity for a one per cent price rise.
notes.explanation: Quantity demanded falls when price rises for almost any good, but it falls more for some goods than for others, and this measure captures the difference.
notes.example: Like a thermometer for price sensitivity: it shows whether a 1% rise loses a firm a sliver of sales or a large share of them.
notes.evidence: A good's price elasticity of demand ( E d {\displaystyle E_{d}} , PED ) is a measure of how sensitive the quantity demanded is to its price.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: When is demand for a good said to be elastic?
notes.back: When its price elasticity is greater than one in absolute value.
notes.explanation: The lead drops the words “in absolute value” here, but the article reads elasticities ignoring the minus sign, so −2 counts as elastic: quantity falls twice as much, in percentage terms, as price rises.
notes.example: Like one brand of baked beans among many on a shelf: a small price rise sends many buyers to another tin.
notes.evidence: Demand for a good is said to be elastic when the elasticity is greater than one. A good with an elasticity of −2 has elastic demand because quantity demanded falls twice as much as the price increase
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: When is demand for a good said to be inelastic?
notes.back: When its price elasticity is less than one in absolute value.
notes.explanation: Price changes then have a relatively small effect on quantity demanded: at −0.5, quantity falls by half as much as the price rises.
notes.example: Like tap water to a household: a higher bill barely changes how much is used.
notes.evidence: Demand for a good is said to be inelastic when the elasticity is less than one in absolute value: that is, changes in price have a relatively small effect on the quantity demanded.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: What does cross elasticity of demand (XED) measure?
notes.back: The effect of a change in one good's price on the quantity demanded of another good.
notes.explanation: Demand for a good depends not only on its own price but also on the prices of related goods.
notes.example: Like price elasticity of demand, but looking sideways: how a rise in the price of tea changes sales of coffee.
notes.evidence: the cross (or cross-price ) elasticity of demand ( XED ) measures the effect of changes in the price of one good on the quantity demanded of another good.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Cross elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: What is a fixed cost?
notes.back: A business expense that does not depend on how many goods or services the business produces; also called an indirect or overhead cost.
notes.explanation: Such costs tend to recur, such as interest or rent paid each month, and tend also to be capital costs.
notes.example: Like a phone contract's monthly line rental, a printer's lease on its press is due whether it prints ten jobs or a thousand.
notes.evidence: fixed costs , also known as indirect costs or overhead costs , are business expenses that are not dependent on the level of goods or services produced by the business.

notes.front: What is a variable cost?
notes.back: A volume-related cost, paid per quantity produced.
notes.explanation: The article adds that variable costs are unknown at the start of the accounting year, since they depend on how much is produced.
notes.example: Like a fixed cost, except it grows with output: the flour a bakery buys rises with every extra batch of loaves.
notes.evidence: This is in contrast to variable costs , which are volume-related (and are paid per quantity produced) and unknown at the beginning of the accounting year.

notes.front: What is the break-even point (BEP)?
notes.back: The point at which total cost and total revenue are equal, so there is neither profit nor loss.
notes.explanation: It can be stated as a sales amount, in units or in revenue, and the article says new ventures use break-even analysis to show potential backers that they could be viable.
notes.example: Like the moment a school fête's takings exactly cover the hire of the marquee and the stock, with nothing left over.
notes.evidence: The break-even point ( BEP ) in economics , business —and specifically cost accounting —is the point at which total cost and total revenue are equal, i.e. "even". In layperson's terms, after all costs are paid for there is neither profit nor loss.

notes.front: What is price discrimination?
notes.back: Selling identical or largely similar goods or services at different prices to different buyers, by perceived market segment.
notes.explanation: It relies on differences in customers' willingness to pay and in the elasticity of their demand.
notes.example: Like a single ticket price for everyone, broken up: a museum charges adults, students and pensioners different amounts for the same entry.
notes.evidence: Price discrimination , known also by several other names, is a microeconomic pricing strategy whereby identical or largely similar goods or services are sold at different prices by the same provider to different buyers, based on which market segment they are perceived to be part of.

notes.front: Among the 4Ps, which is the only element that generates revenue?
notes.back: Price; the article calls the other three cost centres.
notes.explanation: The article adds that the other Ps can reduce price elasticity, which lets price increases drive greater revenue and profit.
notes.evidence: Price is the only revenue generating element among the four Ps, the rest being cost centers . However, the other Ps of marketing will contribute to decreasing price elasticity

notes.front: Where is value-based pricing frequently used?
notes.back: Where the value to the customer is many times the cost of producing the item or service.
notes.explanation: The article's example is software on a disc: making the disc costs about the same whatever is on it, yet prices vary with the value customers perceive.
notes.evidence: This pricing strategy is frequently used where the value to the customer is many times the cost of producing the item or service. For instance, the cost of producing a software CD is about the same independent of the software on it, but the prices vary with the perceived value the customers are expected to have.

notes.front: What is the objective of a price skimming strategy?
notes.back: To capture consumer surplus early in the product life cycle.
notes.explanation: The article says this exploits a monopolistic position or the low price sensitivity of innovators; the practice is also called riding down the demand curve.
notes.evidence: Price skimming is sometimes referred to as riding down the demand curve . The objective of a price skimming strategy is to capture the consumer surplus early in the product life cycle in order to exploit a monopolistic position or the low price sensitivity of innovators.

notes.front: Price skimming is effective only when the firm faces what kind of demand curve?
notes.back: An inelastic demand curve.
notes.explanation: If long-run demand is elastic, the market settles through quantity changes rather than price changes, and the article says penetration pricing then suits better.
notes.evidence: It is effective only when the firm is facing an inelastic demand curve . [ 6 ] If the long-run demand curve is elastic (as in the adjacent diagram), market equilibrium will be achieved by quantity changes rather than price changes. Penetration pricing is a more suitable strategy in this case.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price skimming”, section “Limitations of price skimming”

notes.front: What is the main disadvantage of penetration pricing?
notes.back: It sets long-term price expectations for the product, and image preconceptions for the brand and company.
notes.explanation: The article says this makes it difficult to raise prices later on.
notes.evidence: The main disadvantage with penetration pricing is that it establishes long-term price expectations for the product , and image preconceptions for the brand and company. That makes it difficult to eventually raise prices.

notes.front: How do consumers tend to perceive just-below prices, such as £1.99?
notes.back: As lower than they are: they tend to round down to the next lowest monetary unit.
notes.explanation: A price of $1.99 may therefore be linked, to some degree, with spending $1 rather than $2.
notes.evidence: There is evidence that consumers tend to perceive just-below prices (also referred to as "odd prices") as being lower than they are, tending to round to the next lowest monetary unit.

notes.front: For which kind of products is product bundling most suitable?
notes.back: High-volume, high-margin products, that is, those with low marginal cost.
notes.explanation: Research the article cites found bundling particularly effective for digital information goods with close to zero marginal cost.
notes.evidence: Product bundling is most suitable for high volume and high margin (i.e., low marginal cost) products. Research by Yannis Bakos and Erik Brynjolfsson found that bundling was particularly effective for digital information goods with close to zero marginal cost

notes.front: Must a loss leader be sold below cost?
notes.back: No. It is priced below its minimum profit margin, not necessarily below cost.
notes.explanation: The vendor expects the profit on other goods bought at the same time to produce an overall profit.
notes.evidence: The loss leader is offered at a price below its minimum profit margin, not necessarily below cost .

notes.front: If a good's price elasticity of demand is −2, what happens after a 1% price rise?
notes.back: Quantity demanded falls by about 2%.
notes.explanation: Elasticity gives the percentage change in quantity demanded for a one per cent price rise, holding everything else constant.
notes.evidence: The price elasticity gives the percentage change in quantity demanded when there is a one percent increase in price, holding everything else constant. If the elasticity is −2, that means a one percent price rise leads to a two percent decline in quantity demanded.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: If someone says a good has a price elasticity of 2, what do they almost always mean?
notes.back: An elasticity of −2: price elasticities are negative except in special cases.
notes.explanation: The article treats goods with positive elasticity as rare exceptions to the law of demand, so an unsigned figure is read as negative.
notes.evidence: Price elasticities are negative except in special cases. If a good is said to have an elasticity of 2, it almost always means that the good has an elasticity of −2
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: Total revenue is maximised at the price where the price elasticity of demand is {{c1::unitary (−1)}}.
notes.explanation: At unit elasticity quantity changes by the same percentage as price, so a small price change leaves total revenue unchanged; the lead's "exactly one" means one ignoring the minus sign.
notes.evidence: total revenue is maximized at the combination of price and quantity demanded where the elasticity of demand is unitary.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, section “Effect on entire revenue”

notes.front: Total cost is equal to fixed costs plus {{c1::variable costs}}.
notes.explanation: Costs that stay put whatever the output are fixed, costs that rise with output are variable, and between them they cover every cost.
notes.evidence: Along with variable costs, fixed costs make up one of the two components of total cost: total cost is equal to fixed costs plus variable costs.

notes.front: In the linear cost–volume–profit model, how is the break-even point in units calculated?
notes.back: Total fixed costs ÷ (unit sale price − unit variable cost).
notes.explanation: Setting total revenue equal to total cost and solving for the number of units sold gives this result.
notes.evidence: can be directly computed in terms of Total Revenue (TR) and Total Costs (TC) as: TR = TC P × X = TFC + V × X P × X − V × X = TFC ( P − V ) × X = TFC X = TFC P − V

notes.front: Unit sale price minus unit variable cost is called the {{c1::unit contribution margin}}.
notes.explanation: It is the divisor in the break-even formula, and the article says the break-even point is where contribution equals fixed costs.
notes.evidence: The break-even point can alternatively be computed as the point where Contribution equals Fixed Costs . The quantity, ( P − V ) {\displaystyle \left(P-V\right)} , is of interest in its own right, and is called the Unit Contribution Margin

notes.front: What must a seller have for price discrimination to succeed?
notes.back: Market power.
notes.explanation: The article gives a dominant market share, product uniqueness and sole pricing power as examples of that power.
notes.evidence: For price discrimination to succeed, a seller must have market power, such as a dominant market share, product uniqueness, sole pricing power, etc.

notes.front: What is first-degree price discrimination?
notes.back: Personalised pricing: selling to each customer at a different price, ideally the most each will pay.
notes.explanation: In its perfect form the seller captures the entire consumer surplus of each individual buyer.
notes.evidence: "Personalized pricing" (or first-degree price differentiation) – selling to each customer at a different price; this is also called one-to-one marketing .
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price discrimination”, section “First degree: perfect price discrimination”

notes.front: In second-degree price discrimination, what makes the price of the same good vary?
notes.back: The quantity demanded; it usually takes the form of a quantity discount.
notes.explanation: Diminishing marginal utility means a buyer may not take an extra unit without a discount, so the discount captures some consumer surplus.
notes.evidence: In second-degree price discrimination, the price of the same good varies according to the quantity demanded. It usually comes in the form of a quantity discount that exploits the law of diminishing marginal utility .
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price discrimination”, section “Second degree: quantity discount”

notes.front: In third-degree price discrimination, which group of consumers is charged the higher price?
notes.back: The group with the less elastic demand.
notes.explanation: Groups are split by their different elasticities of demand, and those less sensitive to price can be charged more.
notes.evidence: Third-degree price discrimination means charging a different price to a group of consumers based on their different elasticities of demand: the less elastic group is charged a higher price.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price discrimination”, section “Third degree: market segregation”

notes.front: A premium outdoor-clothing brand keeps its long-run high-price approach, but a regional manager cuts prices on last season's jackets for two weeks to clear surplus stock. What is the price cut?
notes.back: A: a pricing tactic within the broad strategy.
notes.choices:
A) A pricing tactic within the broad strategy
B) A change of pricing strategy
C) Penetration pricing
D) Price lining
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the long-run approach is unchanged. C sets a low launch price for a new product to win share. D limits products to a small number of price points.
notes.explanation: Tactics are shorter-term prices for specific goals, such as clearing surplus inventory, and line managers may vary prices within the strategic approach.
notes.evidence: Tactical pricing decisions are shorter term prices, designed to accomplish specific short-term goals. The tactical approach to pricing may vary from time to time, depending on a range of internal considerations (e.g. such as the need to clear surplus inventory)

notes.front: A candle maker's materials, labour and overheads come to £40 a unit, and it applies a 25% markup using cost-plus pricing. What is the price?
notes.choicesExplained: A is the cost alone, with no markup. B adds 25 pounds rather than 25 per cent. D is only the markup, not the price.
notes.explanation: Cost-plus adds the costs together and applies the markup percentage to them: £40 × 1.25 = £50.
notes.evidence: the direct material cost, direct labor cost, and overhead costs for a product are added together, and a markup percentage is applied (to create a profit margin) in order to derive the price of the product.

notes.front: A firm launches a novel high-end camera. Early enthusiasts are keen to be first and insensitive to price, and the firm wants to recoup development costs before rivals arrive. Which launch strategy fits?
notes.back: C: price skimming.
notes.choices:
A) Penetration pricing
B) Loss leader
C) Price skimming
D) Captive pricing
notes.choicesExplained: A starts low to win share fast, giving up the premium these buyers would pay. B prices one item low to sell other goods. D relies on buyers needing add-ons after a cheap base product.
notes.explanation: Capturing the extra profit of a high launch price lets a firm recoup its sunk costs quicker, before new competition enters and lowers the market price.
notes.evidence: By following this price skimming method and capturing the extra profit, a firm is able to recoup its sunk costs quicker as well as profit off of a higher price in the market before new competition enters and lowers the market price.

notes.front: A new supermarket own-brand energy drink enters a crowded market where shoppers switch readily on price. The firm wants a large share quickly and scale economies. Which launch strategy fits?
notes.back: A: penetration pricing.
notes.choices:
A) Penetration pricing
B) Price skimming
C) Price lining
D) Psychological pricing
notes.choicesExplained: B works only with inelastic demand, and here buyers are price-sensitive. C limits a range to a few price points. D concerns just-below price endings, not a launch strategy.
notes.explanation: Penetration pricing is most commonly tied to the objectives of enlarging market share and exploiting economies of scale or experience.
notes.evidence: Penetration pricing is most commonly associated with marketing objectives of enlarging market share and exploiting economies of scale or experience.

notes.front: A kitchen-knife maker sells a basic, a professional and a chef's-edition set, each at a clearly higher price, so buyers read the tiers as rising quality. Which approach is this?
notes.back: A: product line pricing.
notes.choices:
A) Product line pricing
B) Captive pricing
C) Product bundling
D) Cost-plus pricing
notes.choicesExplained: B needs a cheap base product that forces later purchases. C sells several items as one package. D sets each price from cost plus a markup, not from the tier signal.
notes.explanation: Product line pricing separates products in one category into price groups to create different quality levels in customers' minds.
notes.evidence: It is a process that traders adopt to separate products in the same category into various price groups, to create different quality levels in the customers’ minds.

notes.front: A gift shop prices every one of its 300 items at £5, £10 or £20, which makes stock easy to price and takings easy to forecast. Which approach is this?
notes.back: C: price lining.
notes.choices:
A) Psychological pricing
B) Price discrimination
C) Price lining
D) Loss leader
notes.choicesExplained: A uses just-below endings, and these are round prices. B charges different buyers different prices for the same item. D sells one item below its profit margin to lift other sales.
notes.explanation: Pricing many products at a limited number of prices eases administration and makes customers and profits easier to predict.
notes.evidence: Price lining is a method of pricing different products for a limited number of prices. This strategy allows ease of administering and companies are able to predict their markets of customers and profits much easier.

notes.front: An electric toothbrush sells for very little, but it only works with the maker's replacement heads, which are priced high. Which approach is this?
notes.back: D: captive pricing.
notes.choices:
A) Loss leader
B) Price skimming
C) Product bundling
D) Captive pricing
notes.choicesExplained: A draws buyers to other, unrelated goods rather than to add-ons the product needs. B starts high and lowers price over time. C sells items together as one package.
notes.explanation: The low price of the basic product is recovered from the additional items buyers must purchase to get its full value.
notes.evidence: Although the retailer might lose profit on the first sales item, they will manage to gain it back from the additional products that customers buy.

notes.front: A study finds the price elasticity of demand for a prescription-only medicine is −0.3. How is its demand described?
notes.back: C: inelastic.
notes.choices:
A) Unit elastic
B) Elastic
C) Inelastic
D) Perfectly elastic
notes.choicesExplained: B needs an absolute value above one. A needs an absolute value of exactly one. D is the extreme case in which even a small price rise cuts quantity demanded to zero.
notes.explanation: An absolute value below one means price changes have a relatively small effect on the quantity demanded.
notes.evidence: Demand for a good is said to be inelastic when the elasticity is less than one in absolute value: that is, changes in price have a relatively small effect on the quantity demanded.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price elasticity of demand”, lead section

notes.front: When the price of printers rises, sales of printer paper fall. What does this say about the cross elasticity of demand between them?
notes.back: B: it is negative, so they are complements.
notes.choices:
A) Positive, so they are substitutes
B) Negative, so they are complements
C) Zero, so they are unrelated
D) Positive, so they are complements
notes.choicesExplained: A would need paper sales to rise when printer prices rise. C would need no change in paper sales. D pairs a positive sign with complements, but a positive sign denotes substitutes.
notes.explanation: With complements, a rise in one good's price reduces demand for the other, because the two are used together.
notes.evidence: A negative cross elasticity denotes two products that are complements , while a positive cross elasticity denotes two products are substitutes . If products A and B are complements, an increase in the price of B leads to a decrease in the quantity demanded for A
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Cross elasticity of demand”, section “Results for main types of goods”

notes.front: A furniture workshop lists four costs. Which one is a variable cost?
notes.back: A: timber bought for each chair made.
notes.choices:
A) Timber bought for each chair made
B) Interest on a bank loan
C) Annual insurance on the building
D) Monthly rent on the workshop
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are paid whatever the output, so they are fixed costs; the article names rent and interest as typical examples.
notes.explanation: Variable costs are volume-related and paid per quantity produced, while fixed costs do not depend on the level of output.
notes.evidence: They tend to be recurring, such as interest or rents being paid per month. These costs also tend to be capital costs. This is in contrast to variable costs , which are volume-related (and are paid per quantity produced)

notes.front: A small brewery has fixed costs of £12,000 a month. Each case sells for £50 and has a variable cost of £20. How many cases must it sell a month to break even?
notes.back: A: 400 cases.
notes.choices:
A) 400 cases
B) 600 cases
C) 240 cases
D) 171 cases
notes.choicesExplained: C divides fixed costs by the price and ignores variable cost. B divides by the variable cost instead of the margin. D divides by price plus variable cost.
notes.explanation: Break-even units are fixed costs divided by the unit contribution margin: £12,000 ÷ (£50 − £20) = 400.
notes.evidence: where: TFC is Total Fixed Costs , P is Unit Sale Price , and V is Unit Variable Cost . The break-even point can alternatively be computed as the point where Contribution equals Fixed Costs .

notes.front: A theme park charges the same ride pass at a lower price to school groups than to adults, based on how price-sensitive each group is. Which kind of price discrimination is this?
notes.back: C: third degree.
notes.choices:
A) Second degree
B) First degree
C) Third degree
D) None: it is product differentiation
notes.choicesExplained: B sets a separate price for each individual customer. A varies price with quantity bought. D is wrong because the pass is the same product, with no difference in production cost.
notes.explanation: Third-degree discrimination charges groups different prices according to their elasticities of demand, with the less elastic group paying more.
notes.evidence: Third-degree price discrimination means charging a different price to a group of consumers based on their different elasticities of demand: the less elastic group is charged a higher price.
notes.source: Wikipedia, “Price discrimination”, section “Third degree: market segregation”

notes.front: How does a pricing strategy differ from a pricing tactic?
notes.back: A strategy is the broad, long-term approach that guides price-setters; a tactic is a shorter-term price for a specific short-term goal.
notes.explanation: The strategy typically becomes part of the long-term strategic plan, and many tactics may be used within it in a single year.
notes.evidence: This pricing strategy typically becomes part of the company's overall long-term strategic plan . The strategy is designed to provide broad guidance for price-setters

notes.front: How does pure bundling differ from mixed bundling?
notes.back: Under pure bundling buyers take the whole bundle or nothing; under mixed bundling they may buy the bundle or its separate parts.
notes.explanation: The article also splits pure bundling into joint bundling and leader bundling, and names mixed-leader bundling as a further variant.
notes.evidence: Pure bundling occurs when a consumer can only purchase the entire bundle or nothing at all.

notes.front: What distinguishes price discrimination from product differentiation?
notes.back: In product differentiation the differently priced products differ in production cost; in price discrimination they are identical or largely similar.
notes.explanation: Different prices alone do not make discrimination: the test the article gives is whether production cost differs between the versions.
notes.evidence: Price discrimination is distinguished from product differentiation by the difference in production cost for the differently priced products involved in the latter strategy.

notes.front: What is the overriding factor in determining a good's price elasticity of demand?
notes.back: Buyers' willingness and ability, after a price change, to put off buying and search for substitutes: “wait and look”.
notes.explanation: The listed determinants follow from it: close substitutes, a narrow definition of the good and, for most goods, a longer timespan raise elasticity, while necessity, brand loyalty and someone else paying lower it.
notes.evidence: The overriding factor in determining the elasticity is the willingness and ability of consumers after a price change to postpone immediate consumption decisions concerning the good and to search for substitutes ("wait and look").

notes.front: A café sells one brand of bottled water. Which change would most likely make demand for that brand more price elastic?
notes.back: B: several close rival brands appear beside it on the shelf.
notes.choices:
A) Customers become strongly loyal to the brand
B) Several close rival brands appear beside it on the shelf
C) Most purchases are charged to employers' expense accounts
D) The café becomes the only place selling drinks for miles
notes.choicesExplained: A makes demand more inelastic, because loyalty can override sensitivity to price. C makes it more inelastic, because the buyer does not pay directly. D removes substitutes, so the substitution effect is small and demand inelastic.
notes.explanation: The more and closer the substitutes, the more easily buyers switch after even a small price rise, so elasticity is likely to be higher.
notes.evidence: The more and closer the substitutes available, the higher the elasticity is likely to be, as people can easily switch from one good to another if an even minor price change is made
